steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey of our recent work on automating induction inside saturation-based first-order theorem provers. Position it against prior work on inductive theorem proving and give a section-by-section list of contributions.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The theory of inductively defined data types, like natural numbers (e.g. see Figure 1 (a)), is a commonly used theory when developing imperative/functional programs. So automating reasoning in formal verification also needs automating induction. Previous works on automating induction mostly focus on inductive theorem proving, which decides when induction should be applied and which induction axiom should be used. Recent advances related to automating inductive reasoning, like first-order reasoning with inductively defined data types, inductive strengthening and structural induction in superposition, open new possibilities for automating induction. In this paper we survey our recent results on automating inductive reasoning for first-order properties with inductively defined data types and more.

Relation to the state-of-the-art. Our work automates induction by putting it directly into the saturation-based approach of first-order provers. These provers do saturation-based proof search using the superposition calculus. They also rely on powerful indexing algorithms, notions of redundancy, selection functions and term orderings to make theorem proving efficient. First-order theorem provers complement SMT solvers when reasoning with theories and quantifiers, as shown in the annual system competitions of SMT solvers and of first-order provers.

Our approach to automating induction is conceptually different from previous attempts to use induction with superposition, because we are not restricted to specific clause splitting algorithms and heuristics, and we are not limited to induction over inductively defined data types using a subterm ordering. So we stay within the standard saturation framework and we do not have to introduce constraint clauses or additional predicates, or change the notion of redundancy as in that work. Also, our approach can automate induction over arbitrary data types, not just inductively defined ones, for example integers (Section 9). Our work is also fundamentally different from rewrite-based approaches to automating induction, because we do not rely on external algorithms/heuristics to generate subgoals/lemmas of an inductive property. Instead, applications of induction are inference rules of the saturation process, which add instances of appropriate induction schemata. We extend superposition reasoning with new inference rules that capture inductive steps (Sections 5 - 7), and we optimize the saturation theorem proving process with induction. We also instantiate induction axioms with logically stronger versions of the property we are proving and use induction hypotheses as specialized rewrite rules (Section 8).

Combining saturation with induction like this is very powerful. Our experiments show that our work can solve many problems that no system could solve before, some of them with very complex proofs of program properties and proofs of complex mathematical properties (Section 10). Some of these proofs have over 100 applications of induction among tens of thousands of superposition inferences.

Contributions. This paper is a survey of our recent progress in automating induction using a first-order theorem prover.

- We give a small tutorial of induction in saturation, which helps non-experts in theorem proving understand and use our methodology. For this we describe saturation theorem proving and the main concepts of saturation with induction (Sections 4 - 5).

- We give an overview of the technical considerations for making saturation with induction an efficient approach (Section 5). We discuss variants of induction inference rules over inductively defined data types (Section 6) and over integers (Section 9).

- We present extensions of induction inference rules with multiple premises (Section 7), generalizations and integer reasoning (Section 8).

- We report on exhaustive experiments that compare and analyse our approach against state-of-the-art methods (Section 10).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
One commonly used theory in the development of imperative/functional programs is the theory of inductively defined data types, such as natural numbers (e.g. see Figure 1 (a)). Automating reasoning in formal verification therefore also requires automating induction. Previous works on automating induction mainly focus on inductive theorem proving [1,2,3,4,5]: deciding when induction should be applied and which induction axiom should be used. Recent advances related to automating inductive reasoning, such as first-order reasoning with inductively defined data types [6], inductive strengthening [7] and structural induction in superposition [8,9,10,11,12], open up new possibilities for automating induction. In this paper we survey our recent results towards automating inductive reasoning for first-order properties with inductively defined data types and beyond.

Relation to the state-of-the-art. Our work automates induction by integrating it directly in the saturation-based approach of first-order provers [13,14,15]. These provers implement saturation-based proof search using the superposition calculus [16]. Moreover, they rely on powerful indexing algorithms, notions of redundancy, selection functions and term orderings to make theorem proving efficient. First-order theorem provers complement SMT solvers in reasoning with theories and quantifiers, as evidenced in the annual system competitions of SMT solvers [17,18] and first-order provers [19].

Our approach towards automating induction is conceptually different from previous attempts to use induction with superposition [8,9,12], as we are neither restricted to specific clause splitting algorithms and heuristics [9], nor limited to induction over inductively defined data types using a subterm ordering [12]. As a result, we stay within the standard saturation framework and do not need to introduce constraint clauses or additional predicates, nor change the notion of redundancy as in [12]. In addition, our approach can be used to automate induction over arbitrary, and not just inductively defined, data types, such as integers (Section 9). Our work is also fundamentally different from rewrite-based approaches automating induction [1,2,5,3,7,4], as we do not rely on external algorithms/heuristics to generate subgoals/lemmas of an inductive property. Instead, applications of induction become inference rules of the saturation process, adding instances of appropriate induction schemata. We extend superposition reasoning with new inference rules capturing inductive steps (Sections 5 - 7), and optimize the saturation theorem proving process with induction. We further instantiate induction axioms with logically stronger versions of the property being proved and use induction hypotheses as specialized rewrite rules (Section 8).

This combination of saturation with induction is very powerful. Our experimental results show that many problems previously unsolved by any system can be solved by our work, some of them resulting in very complex proofs of program properties and of complex mathematical properties (Section 10). Some of these proofs involve over 100 applications of induction among tens of thousands of superposition inferences.

Contributions. This paper serves as a survey of our recent progress in automating induction using a first-order theorem prover [10,11,20,21].

- We give a small tutorial of induction in saturation, helping non-experts in theorem proving to understand and further use our methodology. To this end, we describe saturation theorem proving and the main concepts of saturation with induction (Sections 4 - 5).

- We overview the technical considerations for turning saturation with induction into an efficient approach (Section 5). We discuss variants of induction inference rules over inductively defined data types (Section 6) and integers (Section 9).

- We present extensions of induction inference rules with multiple premises (Section 7), generalizations and integer reasoning (Section 8).

- We report on exhaustive experiments comparing and analysing our approach against state-of-the-art methods (Section 10).
